message.reasoning:
I need to write a JUnit 4 test for jsoup's Element class targeting the Defects4J Jsoup-3b bug, aiming for high branch coverage and a good chance of catching the actual fault. I should figure out which bug this is—likely related to wrap(), accumulateParents, or the parents() method.

I'll focus on writing thorough tests covering the constructor, tagName/tag, isBlock, id, attr chaining, parent/parents traversal up to #root, child/children access, and element manipulation methods like appendChild, prependChild, appendElement, and text insertion—since the bug could naturally surface through these core behaviors.

I also need to cover append/prepend HTML parsing, empty(), and wrap() with edge cases—empty string throwing an exception, and wrap returning null when the fragment has no element children. Then there's sibling navigation (next/previous/first/last element sibling), elementSiblingIndex behavior when parent is null, and the various getElementsBy* selector methods that likely rely on Jsoup.parse being available in the test classpath.

Since Jsoup, Tag, Attributes, TextNode, and DataNode are all part of the same source tree, I can use Jsoup.parse(html) to build test documents for things like select() and text(), while using direct Element construction for simpler isolated behaviors like attr() and children(). I still need tests for whitespace-preserving text() inside pre tags, hasText(), data() extraction from script tags, and className/classNames/hasClass handling.

I should also cover addClass, removeClass, toggleClass, val() differences between input and textarea, outerHtml via toString(), html() getter/setter, equals()/hashCode(), and Validate.notNull throwing IllegalArgumentException. Since the full jsoup project source compiles together under Defects4J, I can rely on all these classes being available during test compilation even though the jar itself isn't on the classpath.

Now I'm sketching out ElementTest with the standard imports from Jsoup, nodes, parser, select, and JUnit, then outlining test methods -- starting with a constructor test expecting an IllegalArgumentException when the tag is null, followed by tests for tag name handling.

I'm continuing to plan out the remaining test coverage: block-level checks for div vs span, id handling when unset vs set, attribute chaining, parent traversal (including root exclusion and standalone elements), child/children management with index bounds checking, a basic select query test, and a null-check test for appendChild.

I'm also mapping out tests for append/prepend ordering of elements, text, and HTML nodes, null-handling for appendHtml, an empty() test, and several wrap scenarios covering normal wrapping, wrapping with leftover siblings, empty-string validation, and cases where there's no element to wrap around.

Beyond that, I'm planning coverage for sibling navigation methods—next/previous/first/last element sibling, and sibling index with and without a parent—checking that each returns null or zero appropriately when there's no valid sibling. I'm also sketching out tests for getElementsByTag, getElementById (found and not found), getElementsByClass, getElementsByAttribute, and getElementsByAttributeValue.

Continuing on, I'm listing more attribute-value matching tests (not, starting, ending, containing), index-based filters (less than, greater than, equals), and getAllElements. Then I move into text extraction tests covering simple text, preserve-whitespace for pre tags, and block spacing across multiple children, plus hasText true/false cases, data retrieval, className and classNames getters/setters, hasClass checks, and finally addClass, removeClass, and toggleClass behavior for both adding when absent and removing when present.

I continue the numbered plan with val getters/setters for input and textarea elements, html getter/setter, toString, equals, and hashCode tests. Before writing the actual test code, I want to verify the real API signatures I'll need — Tag.valueOf being static, the Attributes class constructor and put/hasKey/get methods, TextNode and DataNode public constructors taking text/data and baseUri, Document.body() returning an Element, and Parser.parseBodyFragment for building test documents.

For building element hierarchies manually, I'm constructing elements with Tag.valueOf and appendChild to set up parent-child relationships, and for parent() testing I'll rely on Jsoup.parse to get a real document tree since Document's root uses the "#root" tag internally. I plan to parse a simple nested HTML snippet and navigate through it to verify the hierarchy.

Tracing through parents() on a deeply nested p element, the chain should be p -> div -> body -> html, excluding the root since its tagName is "#root" -- that gives me a clean test case. For the wrap() test, I'll need an actual parent-child structure in place first since wrap relies on parentNode.replaceChild, so I'm planning to parse real HTML to get a properly linked p element before testing wrap.

For wrapping with extra sibling markup, the first element in the wrap content becomes the direct replacement while any remainder gets nested inside it as the new deepest child -- I'm verifying that logic traces correctly through replaceChild and addChild calls.

The remainder's parent is actually the fragment body from parsing, so removing it there and appending to the wrap div means the div ends up containing both the original element and the span, with that div sitting in place of the original element in the body.

I should also verify edge cases: an empty wrap string should throw via Validate.notEmpty, and wrapping with a fragment that's just plain text (no elements) should make wrapChildren empty, so wrap() returns null since Elements.first() on an empty list returns null.

I can test this with a standalone element that has no parent at all, since the null-return happens before parentNode is touched -- no NPE expected.

Next, I want to check what happens when accessing a child index that's out of bounds, since children() is an ArrayList-backed structure.

For select(), I should verify tests by parsing simple HTML and confirming the right number of matches come back, both via Document.select and directly on a child Element. Similar tests apply for getElementsByTag and related lookups.

For class-related methods like hasClass, addClass, removeClass, and toggleClass, I can test these on a standalone Element since the Attributes object works independently of any parent node. I'm now thinking through how to test val() next, which requires setting up a text-type Tag.

For val() I need to cover both textarea and input cases—textarea's val() should mirror text() output, while input's val() should read from the value attribute; the setter form needs similar verification in reverse. I also need to build text()-related tests using manually constructed trees of TextNode, DataNode, and Element, including checking whether pre tags preserve whitespace during text() normalization.

I'm thinking through the key detail that the public text() method always trims the final result regardless of the preserveWhitespace flag, while internal whitespace handling depends on that flag—so for pre tags, internal spacing stays intact but leading/trailing whitespace still gets trimmed off the final output.

For regular elements like div, text() normalizes runs of whitespace into single spaces. I'm also verifying hasText() behavior and confirming that data() correctly retrieves raw content from script elements via DataNode.

For equals()/hashCode(), I should test self-equality, null comparisons, and non-Element comparisons returning false, but I'm uncertain about the exact internal logic without seeing the source—I shouldn't guess at behavior that isn't documented.

I'll stick to minimal, verifiable tests instead: self-equality, inequality with a non-Element object, inequality with null, and hashCode consistency across repeated calls on the same object. For equality between differently-tagged elements, I'm tracing through the equals method's logic step by step—checking reference equality, instanceof, then the super.equals call—to see which branches I can safely test without assuming unknown internals of Node.equals.

Given the uncertainty around Node.equals(), I'll limit testing to the clear-cut branches: self-equality and non-instance comparisons returning false. The deeper tag-mismatch branch depends on unverified superclass behavior, so I'll skip asserting strict outcomes there rather than guess.

For Tag equality specifically, jsoup commonly pools Tag instances by name via valueOf, making reference equality hold even without a custom equals override. Since the Tag class source isn't provided, I'll add a light test creating two elements with the same tag name and attributes, checking equals(), while documenting that this relies on an assumption about jsoup's known implementation rather than the given source.

I also need to account for how Attributes handles missing keys—looking at id(), attr() can return null, so get() likely returns null when a key is absent, and I should test accordingly.

I'll keep the test coverage focused on what's directly visible in the Element source, relying on the standard jsoup helper classes (Tag, Attributes, TextNode, DataNode, Document, Parser, Jsoup, Elements, Selector) since those are already required dependencies for Element to compile. Now I'm ready to write the final test file with correct API calls matching the typical defects4j Jsoup project structure.

I should also check how Validate.notEmpty behaves for empty strings in methods like wrap or getElementsByTag, since that throws IllegalArgumentException for null or empty input. Now I'll structure the test file with setUp as needed and write roughly 50 grouped test methods covering these cases thoroughly.

I need to test parents() with recursive accumulation across multiple nesting levels, and elementSiblingIndex returning 0 for a standalone element without a parent. For firstElementSibling and lastElementSibling, there's a suspicious edge case: when siblings.size() is exactly 1, the ternary condition fails and returns null instead of the element itself, which looks like it could be the actual bug in this Defects4J case — I want to write a targeted test for this single-child scenario.

Since the point of this test is to catch the actual fault, I should write the assertion based on the correct expected behavior from the spec, so the test fails against the buggy implementation and successfully exposes the defect—that's exactly the goal here.

Looking at the javadoc for firstElementSibling, it should return the parent's first element child, so if this element is an only child, it should return itself.

Based on this, I'm confident the buggy code returns null in that single-child case, which contradicts the contract - this matches a known Jsoup defect pattern. I'll write assertions expecting the element itself rather than null for firstElementSibling and lastElementSibling when they're the only child, since these tests should fail against the buggy implementation and pass against a correct one.

For nextElementSibling and previousElementSibling, the index-validation logic looks safe since the element should always be found in its parent's children list, so that's not a bug area. I'm now finalizing the code along with comments explaining the fault-detection rationale, then I'll write up the complete answer with a summary table in Thai, double-checking method signatures like Attributes.put and hasKey, plus noting the edge case where splitting an empty class string yields a set containing an empty string.

Actually this contradicts the javadoc which says classNames() should return an empty set when there's no class attribute, but the real behavior returns a single-element set with an empty string instead. That's a second potential fault worth testing against the documented contract, so I want to include a test for it too, while being careful not to make the whole test suite centered on that one issue.

I'll aim for a balance—mostly tests that validate the actual implementation behavior as documented, plus a couple that intentionally check the spec-based expectations where known faults exist, with comments noting these could signal defects.

Now I'm assembling the complete test file, pulling in the necessary jsoup and JUnit imports, and writing the final code to ensure it compiles correctly.

I won't assert on whether id() can return null internally, just test observable behavior: default empty string, then set value after attr(). Confirming Tag.valueOf and related Tag methods match the expected API, then starting to write the wrap test using a parsed document with a body and paragraph element.

Writing wrap test assertions...

Now drafting the remainder-wrapping test, checking that body keeps only the outer div while the span becomes its sibling inside, then starting a test that expects wrap() to throw when the element has no parent.

I'm verifying wrap() throws for empty input, returns null when no tag is found in the wrapping html, then checking that append/prepend correctly insert multiple sibling elements in order, with append rejecting null input. Next I'm setting up a parse test to check getElementsByTag against an element with a class attribute.

For getElementsByAttributeValueNot, I'm reasoning that it matches elements lacking the attribute or holding a different value - so the div itself qualifies since it has no id, while the pid paragraph is excluded for matching exactly, leaving the div, second paragraph, and anchor as the three results.

Given uncertainty around Collector's exact inclusive/exclusive traversal semantics, I'll keep the assertions loose - just confirm the pid element is absent and the div is present, rather than asserting precise counts.

Most of these getElementsBy* methods are thin delegations to Collector, so the main coverage goal is just hitting the Validate.notEmpty checks for null/empty keys plus confirming a normal call doesn't throw.

For getElementsByTag and getElementById, I'll add a basic check since they contain extra branching logic that returns an element when found versus null otherwise. The remaining methods are simple one-liners with no internal branching, so I'll just call them for method coverage with not-null assertions rather than heavy logic checks.

Since the priority is branch coverage, I should really concentrate on methods with real conditional paths: id(), the parent-accumulation loop, children() iteration, wrap's null checks and multi-child loop, the sibling navigation methods with their if/else and ternary branches, and text()'s traversal loop with multiple conditions.

I'm mapping out the nested branches in text-handling methods -- distinguishing TextNode vs Element children, toggling preserveWhitespace, tracking lastCharIsWhitespace, and the compound condition checking block status and whitespace. I also need to cover preserveWhitespace()'s own OR-condition, hasText()'s loop with early-return vs continue paths, and className()/classNames()'s caching logic where I'd need to call it twice to exercise both the initialization and cached-reuse branches.

Given the remaining branches -- addClass/removeClass/toggleClass's if/else, val()'s textarea-vs-other check, outerHtml's multiple compound conditions around block status and canContainBlock(), and equals()'s chain of null/type checks -- I'm prioritizing which test scenarios will hit the most branch points efficiently, starting with toString()/outerHtml() across block vs inline elements and empty vs child-containing tags.

I'll test "img" as an empty inline tag that should self-close, a block div with text content to check the children/indent path, and "span" as an inline non-empty tag with no children to confirm it renders as open/close pair rather than self-closing.

Given the uncertainty around indent() formatting, I'll favor "contains" assertions over exact string matches to keep tests robust against whitespace differences, focusing on structural correctness rather than precise output. I'm aiming for roughly 45-55 test methods total, using Jsoup.parse to construct Document contexts, and need to double check Element exposes a siblingIndex() method before relying on it.

I also want to confirm Elements supports get(int) and size() through its ArrayList inheritance, and that Document's internal tag name is "#root" to match my parent-accumulation checks. With those confirmed, I'm writing out the complete, well-organized test class with grouped comments by section, and considering whether to test preserveWhitespace() given its default access modifier.

Since preserveWhitespace() is package-private, placing the test class in org.jsoup.nodes itself lets me call it directly without reflection, which matches typical conventions for this kind of test suite. I'll declare the test file under that same package.

I'll finalize the test in the org.jsoup.nodes package, importing Jsoup, Tag, and Elements from their respective packages to demonstrate proper usage, then write out the full test.
